p: You know and it's not just me. Like, Mikey got his the year before me, so now we're in the same building. Wow, how, how great, right? We're so lucky to have that. At least, but things happen on the street. As you're waiting, I mean, I was in a van. Nobody knew I was in a van. Nobody could imagine I was in a van. At the time, I had a very, very successful YouTube channel, and I guarantee you, not one of my subscribers knew that that's what I was going through. You can't judge people on the way that they look. You have no idea what they're going through. Nothing. And when they get to the street, when you're on the street level, anything can happen from there. Please find your seats. We’re ready to begin. Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Welcome to the New York City Council hearing on the Taskforce to Combat Antisemitism. At this time, please find your seats and please do not approach the dais. If you are testifying today, fill out a slip with the Sergeants at the back. And also, silence your electronics. Thank you for your cooperations. Chairs, you may begin.

Okay, good afternoon, everyone. I’m Council Member Inna Vernikov, Co-Chair of the Taskforce to Combat Antisemitism. First, I would like to thank our Co-Chair, Council Member Eric Dinowitz for joining me in heading up the first-ever hearing of this newly established taskforce entitled Reporting on Antisemitism Hate Crimes and Bias Incidents in New York City. I also want to thank the Council’s Jewish Caucus and the members of this taskforce for recognizing the urgency of this moment and for meeting that urgency with concrete action. I want to begin by sharing something personal and talk about why this taskforce is so important to me. I was born

in the Ukraine which was part of the former Soviet Union. My family, like thousands of families I am privileged to represent came to this country as refugees, many escaping institutionalized antisemitism. We know what it looks like when hatred of the Jewish people is tolerated, normalized, and allowed to fester. Jews were forced to hide their identities, conduct weather ceremonies, and Jewish rituals in basements, and change their last names. Unfortunately, this virus of Jew hatred is not new to us. Every generation, there is someone who comes for the Jewish people, and every generation the Jewish people persevere. This country and this city gave us what no other place on earth did. It gave us freedom, freedom to worship and practice as we wish, and freedom to be proud of who we are, freedom from harassment, intimidation, and persecution for simply being born a Jew. And yet, here we are in New York City at a critical moment. With hate crimes and bias incidents against the Jewish community making up over half of all suspected hate crimes in New York City. That means the Jewish community experiences more hate crimes than all other communities combined, even as Jews make up only 10 percent– around 10 percent of

the city’s population. In 2025, a suspected anti-Jewish incident was occurring every 26 hours. The average number of anti-Jewish hate crimes per month in New York City has risen steadily from 17 incidents per month in 2021 to nearly 29 per month in 2024. Antisemitic assaults have increased by a staggering 583 percent over the past five years. So, I ask, how long are we going to allow this to continue? And where do we think this will all lead? I want to be clear, antisemitism is not just a problem for the Jews. It is a rot that spreads through the fabric of a society. I will not allow that same rot to take hold here in this city that I love which has the largest diaspora Jewish community in the world. And that is why I’m committed to calling it out and tackling it no matter where it comes from, the right or the left, from near or far. It’s often easy to condemn antisemitism of your opponent or from the other side of the political, and we all do that plenty. But I know that it takes more courage to also stand up and denounce it when it comes from your own party. We must do so anyway because it is the right thing to do. There are hundreds if not thousands of recent incidents we can

list, but just two nights ago there was an incident in my district where a group of masked protestors decided to march outside a day school and a house of worship, intimidate children and their parents trying to pick them up from daycare. Two-year-olds were crying while grown adults with their faces covered shouted at them. Police were present, but unfortunately, no safe distance between the protest activity and synagogue and daycare was created. There was no political activity occurring inside the school. It was mid-day on a Monday when children should feel safe and carefree in their schools. A rabbi was inside the synagogue preparing a boy for his bar mitzvah. Protestors were too cowardly to even show their faces, shouted in a clear attempt to intimidate worshipers and children. Is this acceptable? Do we think this should be normalized. The world once looked away and saw the annihilation of millions of innocent people. This taskforce was created, because we refuse to look away. Our job is to understand what is happening with hate crimes and bias incidents in the city, what is being reported, what is not being reported, why, and what we intend to do about it. I am proud to chair this taskforce

and proud that this taskforce is comprised of a diverse group of Council Members who may disagree on many things, but who agree that we cannot and will not ignore the virus of Jew hatred. I’m thankful to the city agencies and offices– to the District Attorney’s Office who have joined us here to discuss this incredibly critical issue. And I’m committed to making sure that when we leave this room today, we’re closer to real answers and real action. Thank you very much, and I would now like to turn over to my Chair, Council Member Dinowitz for his opening remarks.

Thank you, Chair Vernikov, and thank you for sharing, you know, such personal stories about life in the former Soviet Union. It reminds me of my father-in-law who in the 80s took trips to the former Soviet Union to secretly conduct weddings and perform Jewish rituals, and every time he would tell me these stories, I think– you know, you would think that can only happen in a foreign country. In fact, it was happening in a foreign country, but during my time as a teacher, particularly in my last four and a half years of Chair of the Jewish Caucus I’ve witnessed not only an

increase in antisemitism and anti-Jewish incidents around New York City, but quite disturbingly I’ve witnessed too many people in positions of power become increasingly comfortable with staying silent on this issue, comfortable looking the other way, comfortable with providing context or justification to what is blatant hate. That in part, is why I’m so grateful for Speaker Menin’s leadership on the issue for the Jewish Caucus, for the creation of this taskforce, and for my co-chair. I’m grateful that we are sitting here raising our voices on an issue that has been ignored by too many people for far too long. It’s time for us to confront the scourge of antisemitism and stop it dead in its tracks, and in order to do that, we need to be clear-eyed about the problem we are confronting, and we need to understand just how ubiquitous anti-Jewish hate crimes are just how ubiquitous anti-Jewish bias incidents are. My co-chair shared some alarming statistics about the rise and prevalence of anti-Jewish hate crimes, but it’s important not just to talk about these crimes in the context of statistics, but what these crimes mean, because in hate crime, a crime against a Jewish person for their beliefs, for their shared ancestry

is not just an attack on that person, but it’s an attack on that people. It harms the entire community. Now, many of these are missed in the news. They become so normalized that they don’t even get reported on. But just a few examples: In Brooklyn a man drove his vehicles onto the front lawn of a Jewish institution, attempted to run over yeshiva students and teachers while shouting, “I’m going to kill the Jews.” A Jewish woman was sexually harassed with her skirt lifted up and lewd comments made by a perpetrator who stated, “I want to see her ass. She’s Jewish.” In June of last year, an elderly man was punched in face while hanging posters for Israeli hostages while his attacker yelled, “Free Palestine.” That same month, a Jewish man walking home on Shabbat was repeatedly kicked by an assailant who yelled and blamed him for Gaza, and left the man unconscious in the street. In February of this year, a man showed up at a Manhattan synagogue on Shabbat, claiming to be a reincarnation of Adolph Hitler and threatening to kill the worshipers. A child riding a public bus in the Bronx had a driver turn and say to them, “You best not be a f-ing Jew.” Most disturbingly, according to the Antidefamation League, 23 percent of

anti-Jewish incidents that occurred in Brooklyn, which has the largest number of incidents, have involved children, or places frequented by children, including schools and playgrounds. Close to a quarter of incidents in Brooklyn have been targeting our youth, our kids. How can we remain silent? As a former teacher, I know how crucial it is to confront issues directing children directly and to take decisive action to ensure a better future for them. At today’s hearing, we are doing just that. We are here to listen to city agencies and offices responsible for tracking and responding to anti-Jewish incidents and ultimately to the community members who are living this reality. I intend to use taskforce to make sure that my voice as a Council Member, the voice of this City Council leads somewhere meaningful, because throughout our history as people we have seen time and time again the inaction of governments leading to the persecution or eviction of Jewish people and Jewish communities from their homes. And throughout history, they’ve been driven away, but today we will not be the government that sits silently by. We will not be a government of inaction that allows Jews to be persecuted because

we are looking the other way. I want to thank you all for coming today, to the administration, to everyone here who plans to testify and offer testimony, and I want to turn it back to my co-chair, Chair Vernikov.

Thank you, Chair Dinowitz, and I would now like to acknowledge my colleagues on the taskforce who are present with us today, Council Member Hanks, Council Member Maloney, Council Member Epstein, and Council Member Gale Brewer. And in addition to thanking members of the administration and other interested stakeholders, the witnesses who are testifying today, I’d like to thank the Speaker’s Office and also last but not least we would like to thank our respective staff members, Executive Director of Minority Delegation, Peter Spencer, my Legislative Director, Troy Olson [sp?], my Communications Liaison, Karen Kurson [sp?], my Operations Director, Izzy Weiss [sp?], and Chair Dinowitz’s Chief of Staff, Jenna Klaus [sp?], and Legislative Director, Theo Solter [sp?], as well as, Sara Liss [sp?], Special Counsel to the Speaker, and Kristy Dwyer [sp?], Senior Legislative Policy Analyst for the Office of the Special Counsel who helped make

today’s hearing possible. I have to say this is my first time chairing a hearing, and you two are absolutely incredible. Thank you. Before we continue, I would like to remind everyone who wishes to testify in-person today that you must fill out an appearance card which is located on the desk of the Sergeant at Arms near the entrance of this room. Please fill it out even if you’ve already registered to testify in advance. To allow as many people as possible to testify, public testimony will be limited to two minutes per person. I’m also going to ask my colleagues to limit their questions and comments to five minutes each. Please note that witnesses who are here in person will testify before those who are on Zoom. I also want to acknowledge Council Member Felder who is here with us today. And now we are ready to begin. In accordance with the rules of the Council, I will call on the Committee Counsel to administer the affirmation to the witnesses from the administration who are going to give testimony.
Please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
I do.
Thank you. You can begin when you’re ready.

Good afternoon, Chair Vernikov, Chair Dinowitz, and members of the Council’s Taskforce to Combat Antisemitism. My name is Michael Gerber and I’m the Deputy Commissioner of Legal Matters for the NYPD. I’m joined here today by Assistant Chief Andrew Arias, Commanding Officer of the Detective Bureau’s Specialty Enforcement Division. On behalf of Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, we thank you for the opportunity to testify today regarding hate crime reporting. Every day, the NYPD investigates a wide range of crimes across New York City. Among the most infuriating and heart-breaking are hate crimes, offenses in which the victim is targeted because of one or more protected characteristics. These crimes tear at the fabric of society, both through the acts themselves and the underlying hatred that seeks to divide us. We must hold the perpetrators accountable and give our support to the victims, both the individuals targeted and the communities of which they are a part of. As part of this critical shared

work, members of the public need clear, accurate, and timely data about hate crime activity. That data shows that while jews make up roughly 10 percent of New Yorkers, more than 50 percent of the hate crimes in the city in the first quarter of 2026 were classified as anti-Jewish. This was true in 2024 and 2025 as well. Antisemitism has been a source of violence and destruction for a millennia. It is on the rise globally and it is a reality in our city today. That said, our procedures regarding hate crime reporting are the same across all types of hate crime, and so I’m going to speak about those procedures more broadly. When it comes to hate crimes, there are two data sets that are important. One is the set of confirmed hate crimes. After an incident is reported as a possible hate crime, the NYPD Hate Crimes Taskforce, an elite group of detectives, determines whether the incident is properly categorized as a hate crime under governing law and devotes tremendous resources and expertise to bringing those responsible to justice. The number of such confirmed hate crimes cases, where they occurred, the nature of the crimes, and their breakdown by the type of bias at issue is all crucial

information. This confirmed hate crime information is a data of record for the NYPD when it comes to hate crime activity in the city. It is carefully measured and rigorously maintained within department systems and used for crime analysis. It is provided to the state and the FBI for crime reporting purposes and it is shared with the public through the Hate Crimes Dashboard, NYC Open Data, and the Hate Crimes Summary Reports. In particular, the Hate Crimes Dashboard provides this information in a user-friendly manner and enables anyone to review and visualize hate crime data in different ways. The dashboard includes incident level data regarding every confirmed hate crime in New York City and whether arrests have been made in connection with those hate crimes. I want to emphasize that nothing about how we calculate and track confirmed hate crimes has changed at all. There is a second important data set when it comes to hate crimes, and that is reported hate crimes. That is incidents flagged as possible hate crimes for investigation by the taskforce, whether because of information provided by a complainant or witness, observations by control, incidents that have been flagged by communal

organizations or civic leaders or any other reason to refer a case to the taskforce. To be clear, not all of these incidents will be confirmed as hate crimes by the taskforce. As our detectives investigate, they may determine that on the evidence before them and under the requirements of state law, some of these reports cannot be classified as hate crimes. There can be various reasons for this. Sometimes the crime in question is not a specified offense under the New York State Hate Crimes Act, and therefore, even if the crime is bias-based, it cannot be categorized as a hate crime under New York law. Sometimes, our investigation reveals that the victim was not targeted because of a protective characteristic, but for some other reason entirely. And sometimes, it may in fact be a hate crime, but the evidence is not there to support the charge. Indeed, under New York Law, the fact that a victim is a member of a protected class is not legally sufficient without more to charge a hate crime. An individual may perceive that they were the victim of a hate crime, and they may be right, but the law requires more before we can bring that charge. Until this month, the NYPD had not systematically tracked

and had never released to the public the universe of reported hate crimes referred to the taskforce for investigation. This set of possible hate crimes is not the data that we rely on for crime analysis or for state and federal reporting purposes. It is distinct from the confirmed hate crime data that reflects the investigative work of the taskforce. But the data regarding reported hate crimes reflects something else. It captures what victims perceive to be hate crimes. That understanding by the individual victim and by the individual’s community matters. It can result in pain and trauma that is separate and distinct from whether something qualifies as a hate crime. Tracking and sharing data regarding reported hate crimes expresses the significance of this experience by victims and communities. And trends in reported hate crimes are a way of gauging over time how victims in their communities perceive criminal activity. That is, why as the Police Commissioner announced several weeks ago, we are now reporting monthly on both confirmed hate crimes and reported hate crimes. This will enhance– this will enhance transparency and foster public discourse, giving data not only what constitutes hate crimes under the law,

but also on what victims experience as hate crimes. The Department has long prioritized hate crime investigations and the work of the taskforce. But Commissioner Tisch identified a deficiency in our reporting and ordered the Department to correct it. We are proud to take this step which we believe places the NYPD at the forefront of hate crime reporting in the country. I also want to address a change that we made in the beginning of March when we stopped using a data set that we had previously appended to our monthly crime reports. That data did not reflect confirmed hate crimes. It did not reflect reported hate crimes. It as numbers pulled from an informal tracker that had a mix of reported hate crimes that had not been classified by the taskforce and confirmed hate crimes. These were hodge-podge numbers resulting in clarity about nothing. When the Police Commissioner learned how this data was being generated. She directed the Department to stop reporting in this way. That step, like the decision to start sharing reported hate crime numbers as well as confirmed hate crimes was taken at the direction of Commissioner Tisch. As is typical of hate crime– of crime data reporting more generally, these changes

in hate crime reporting were not the initiative or direction of anyone at City Hall. We firmly believe these were the right decisions and we stand by them. That said, we should have done a better job explaining what we were doing and why we were doing it. And on reflection, we should have made the changes at one time rather than in two steps. Anti-Jewish hate crimes are a scourge on our city. The NYPD is proud of its daily relentless efforts to solve these crimes, achieve justice for victims, and keep New Yorkers safe. Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today, and we look forward to answering any questions that you may have.
We’re calling on the DA’s Office to testify. Thank you.

Alright, good afternoon. I want to thank Council Member Inna Vernikov, the Chair, and Co-chair Eric Dinowitz, for the invitation to speak at this inaugural testimony. I am Eric Gonzalez. I’m the District Attorney of Brooklyn, and I am proud to stand with each of you confronting antisemitism in our city. As all of you know, Brooklyn is home to the largest Jewish population of any county in the United States. More

Jewish people live in Brooklyn than anywhere else in the world outside of the state of Israel. That’s a source of pride and it carries significant and serious responsibility. Jewish life in our city and in Brooklyn should be lived openly, proudly and safely. No one should feel afraid riding the subway, wearing their kippah, sending a child to yeshiva, going to shul, visiting friends, opening a Jewish-owned business or celebrating and gathering with friends and neighbors. When that fear takes hold, it harms far more than the immediate victim, as Council Member Dinowitz said, sends a message to an entire community that they are being targeted in the very place they call home. The numbers show how urgent this remains. In 2025, Brooklyn recorded 239 hate crime incidents. Of those, 148, nearly 62 percent, were anti-Semitic. Antisemitism was by far the largest category of hate crimes we confronted in Brooklyn. In the first quarter of 2026, anti-semitic incidents made up more than half of all the hate crimes reported in Brooklyn. Behind those numbers are real people and real fear, parents explaining to children why a swastika was painted near their park, families wondering whether it’s safe to walk to the

synagogue, students and seniors feeling singled out or afraid to wear the Star of David, and community members unsure whether what happened to them should even be reported. My message to the Brooklyn Jewish community is simple and direct, please report all of these incidents. Let the police determine whether this incident is in fact a crime and make the legal determination. Even when a case cannot be prosecuted, reporting helps us identify patterns, deploy resources, support victims and sends the message that this hate will not be ignored. That is why one of the first decision I made as District Attorney was to create New York City’s first standalone Hate Crime Bureau. We staffed it with experienced prosecutors who work with the NYPD Hate Crime Taskforce from the earliest stages of an investigation, because hate crimes require careful evidence gathering. They also require earning trust with the communities we serve and a full understanding of the harms that these incidents cause. And I should also add that hate crimes unlike any other crime, the District Attorney must prove in court the motive behind the crime. In every other crime, it’s significantly– all you have to do is

establish the identity of your offender and the fact that that crime was committed. In the practice of the enhancement of a hate crime, the people have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that the motive was bias of a protected class in whole or in substantial part. I understand that prosecution alone cannot solve this problem. Our office works with community leaders, schools, yashivas, the shomrin [sic], hatzolah [sic], and many others including the ADL. Our partners help us try to educate young people and pursue accountability in these cases that prevent future harm. I should say that this Office of Hate Crimes in my– in the DA’s Office in Brooklyn, was created before the City Council and the Mayor’s Office provided funding to the other District Attorneys to have dedicated Hate Crime Bureaus. I’ve asked the Speaker and I’ve testified during funding that Brooklyn should also have dedicated funding for a Hate Crimes Bureau. We do not receive any dedicated funding. That money would go directly to fight hate crimes. But I want to make it clear to the Jewish community, whether or not the funding is given, I am committed to taking these threats against this community very seriously. We will continue

using every appropriate tool to protect the Jewish New Yorkers and really every community from the scourge of hate crimes. Thank you for the invitation, and I’m happy to answer any questions.

Thank you, DA Gonzalez. I’m not going to ask some questions. After that, I’ll pass it over to my co-chair, and then I think we’ll pass it over to some of our colleagues because have to leave by one. DA Gonzalez, I just want to say that you were invited here today. You did not have to be here, and we invited all five District Attorneys. You are the only one who showed up. We really appreciate it. I think it goes to show to the type of a public servant that you are, that you prioritize transparency and that you take these issues that we’re here today to discuss very seriously, and we very much appreciate it.
Thank you.
Could you talk to us a little bit about the process of how the District Attorney’s Office handles hate crimes from the moment they’re referred from the NYPD?

Sure. It’s an important piece of how we handle hate crimes, very

specifically, and you know, we try to work as closely with the New York City Police Department as possible, from the very inception of when a suspected hate crime happens. Part of the effort is, is when an incident takes place in a precinct, we would ask to be notified of a suspected hate crime that has taken place so that we can make sure that the dedicated hate crime prosecutors and our social workers are immediately made aware. The police will conduct their investigation. We will serve as a sounding board for them when needed in terms of what type of evidence we’re seeking to enhance the case. But also, very specifically, we want to make sure that we’re reaching out to the victim at the earliest possible stage to say the services that we provide in our office, including much of the social work that victims of these horrific crimes require. And then when the case comes in, we work very specifically with the detective that’s assigned the case to make sure that the witnesses are needed for grand jury and all the other evidence is made available, often video. Every single hate crime that’s elevated to a felony is presented to a grand jury in the county as

long as we believe we have the right person in custody.
Thank you. Can you tell us if the Brooklyn DA’s Office has ADAs and other staff who understand sensitivity of Jewish culture and customs, and how many would you say?

Yeah. So, my office, you know, we have over 560 attorneys. There’s a large segment of both attorneys and staff who are Jewish. There’s an affinity group in the office for Jewish staff who are often involved in Jewish life in this city and in my office. But in terms of very specifically dealing with victims of crime, you know, the office makes sure that we have people who speak Hebrew, speak Yiddish. It’s on our website. There’s information, public information made available in, you know, many different languages, and we have people who are very specifically involved– social workers who deal with, you know, Jewish culture and our understanding of the different traditions, customs that are necessary to make people feel comfortable, set of cultural competency. We also have a chaplain, Rabbi Joel Friedman [sp?] who comes into our office very

specifically to talk about holiday traditions, when witnesses are available, when they can’t answer the phone, when they can’t sign a piece of paper because it would be in violation of religious traditions or customs. We try to do the best that we can to make sure that the prosecutors and staff understand, you know, the needs of our community, for example the Sabbath, so that they know when a witness would be able to be spoken to, when they’d be able to be brought downtown. And just like everything else, we have people who are just Jewish who really care to make sure they’re a welcoming face in the office when the victims come in and have that trauma and want to feel like they can talk to someone in their own language or who understands their traditions.
Could you talk to us a little bit about the challenges of prosecuting hate crimes, and specifically antisemitic hate crimes?

Yeah. I think– I started to mention some of the challenges. You know, as some people don’t understand, there is no crime of a hate crime. That’s not a penal law charge. It’s a sentence enhancement. And so what we

do is we look at the incident that took place. Is it eligible to be enhanced as a hate crime, and what we are looking for– so, you know, if someone is being selected or the crime is being committed because of bias, we have to be able to show beyond a reasonable doubt that the motivation in whole or substantial part was created because of the bias, right? So, people being selected and targeted, because they meet protected status or is this a crime that the motivation was simply a dispute that had nothing to do with their protected status. And we work very closely with the detectives. We have analysts in our office that often will look at an accused person’s social media to see what they’re doing on social media, if they’re espousing antisemitic rhetoric to see whether or not that’s a motivating factor. As I testified earlier, hate crimes requires specialization in the prosecutors because it is the only crime where the District Attorney must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the reason that the reason that crime was committed was because of this bias. In every other crime, you just have to establish a crime was committed and the identity of the perpetrator beyond a reasonable doubt. Here, we

have the additional burden of trying to understand what motivated the these attackers for doing what they did.
Thank you. I will now pass it over to my co-chair, Council Member Dinowitz, and we’ll come back to you.

Thank you, Co-chair Vernikov. Deputy Commissioner Gerber, how are you? I want to talk a little bit about what you spoke about in your testimony. You know, someone reports something to the NYPD, and then you say it’s investigated by the Hate Crimes Taskforce. But there’s a step in between that I want to talk a little bit about, and that’s the reporting officer. If someone goes to a precinct to report a crime, or a patrol officer comes to the scene of a crime or an alleged crime– correct me if I’m wrong– it is the reporting officer that then on the spot would determine whether it should be referred to the NYPD Hate Crimes Taskforce.

So, not exactly. So, someone’s making a criminal complaint or patrol’s responding to a scene. There’s some– they’re being told about criminal activity, potential

criminal activity, right? If they perceive it’s maybe a bias incident, maybe bias-related– yeah, they’re not making a determination at this point. Is this a– you know, is it a hate crime? We’re not close to that yet. Then you go up the chain. So, the key is getting a supervisor on scene, then the duty captain is getting called, right? So, the duty captain plays a crucial role in this. It’s an executive, right? A captain who– so they’re coming to the scene, possible bias. Okay. Now, they’re making all sorts of notifications. They’re notifying up their chain, CO, borough commander. They’re notifying Community Affairs. They’re notifying the Hate Crimes Taskforce, and that’s going to set in motion several things, right? So, now Hate Crimes Taskforce is going to investigate. Separate and apart from that investigation, you also have Department executives and Community Affairs are aware that this happened and in a position to respond.

I want to pause. Because you’re talking about, you know, a few steps down the line. I’m talking about the moment someone feels they’re a victim of an active bias. At that moment, it is up to the responding officer to

determine whether to bring it up the chain of command or not, and— I just– you know, I just want to read from the website, and if it’s wrong or we need clarity, this is why this hearing is important. It says the responding officers will provide whatever immediate assistance is needed and begin the reporting process. If the situation is deemed to be a possible bias-motivated incident, the NYPD Hate Crime Taskforce will be notified. So, by reading that, I would assume it’s the responding officer or– or if someone goes to a precinct, the person whom they’re reporting, that would deem whether it is a possible bias-motivated incident. Is that accurate?
So, what I would say is, obviously, it has to get flagged as a possible bias incident by somebody.
Right.

Right? So, that determination, whether it goes over to Hate Crimes Taskforce and it being– you know, notifications are being made, it has to be made by the Duty Captain, but you are right. You are right that initially somebody in some context has to flag

this. Oh, this is a possible bias incident that’s going to require notifications.

Right. So, and I want to pause there, because that’s an important point of, you know, the reporting timeline, the reporting process. Some of the reports we’ve gotten to our office is that people have reported things to various precincts, and the person said, oh, that’s not really– you know, I’ll take it down. It’s not really a hate crime, though. It’s not really a bias incident. And they will fill out the report as such. And the Division of Criminal Justice Services which– from the state, also says if the investigating officer does not identify a bias motivation or does not reflect a bias motivation in the official incident report, the incident will not be reported to DCJS as a hate crime. And so what I’m concerned about– I’m concerned about a lot of things. But right now with these questions is sort of that first step, that responding officer or the responding– or the officer who’s taking in the report, that if we’ve received news to our office or complaints to our office that the officer at that point determined it wasn’t an active bias, it’s not going up the chain.

It’s not going to the taskforce at all for them to determine it.

Alright, so to the extent you have someone, a desk officer, an officer on patrol who is discouraging someone from reporting a hate crime, is being dismissive, is– you know, the person’s saying, hey, I believe this was bias and is ignoring that– I mean, what you’re describing frankly is misconduct, right? Like, that’s not what’s supposed to happen. You know, and what I would say if there are reports like that that come to your office, they should be referred to us, to the Internal Affairs Bureau for investigation, because– I mean, it’s not even– these are not particular the hate crimes, right? To the extent a member of patrol, a member of the department is in any way discouraging hate crime reporting or not taking hate crime report accurately, like– again, like we would investigate that internally, and if that was substantiated, the person would be subject to discipline. So, I mean, to the extent what you’re describing is someone who– you know, when a person comes forward and says– describing a possible bias incident, saying they were the victim of a bias

incident, and then somehow being dismissive of that, that is totally unacceptable and is not what they’re supposed to be doing. It’s not what we stand for. And again, I think if there are complaints of that, they should be referred to us so that IB can investigate.

But there’s also the reality that perhaps the responding officer or the person at the precinct may not be able to identify, and this– just to let you know, this is my last question for now. We’re going to turn it over some committee member questions, and we’ll come back. So there will be more on this. Don’t worry. I can see you were very worried in your face. But to what– it may be the case that that responding officer or the person at the precinct just frankly doesn’t know, can’t identify– doesn’t have the cultural competency to be able to have that same conversation that the victim is having. To what extent is the NYPD training all of its officers to properly identify and to have the cultural competency specific to antisemitism which as we’ve all noted make the vast majority of hate crimes more than any other group combined– to what extent is every single officer

receiving that culturally competent training and identifying acts of antisemitism?
Great question. I’m going to turn it over to Chief Arias to–

Thank you very much, Chair. When it comes to the training of uniformed members of the service in regard to identifying a possible bias incident, the procedure as dictated by our NYPD Patrol Guide is talk to them in the police academy as recruit officers. It is reinforced to them upon promotion to Sergeant, Lieutenant and/or Captain to explain the specific roles from initial uniformed member of the service being contacted by a complainant all the way up to reporting to a supervisor and then the Duty Captain.
You said talk– during their training, talk to them. What does that look like? Is that a 30-second conversation? Is it a Zoom? It is a in-person–
[interposing] No, it is a–
[interposing] What does that training look like?

It is a specific block as part of the curriculum as outlined by the New York Police Department in its recruit training process, in its supervisory leadership development courses to Sergeant, Lieutenant and Captain, and also there is– there are outlines provided by the Hate Crimes Taskforce to members of the Detective Bureau whether in the Hate Crime Taskforce or not and simply in detective squads and other investigative units through the criminal investigator.
And is it part of– is antisemitism specifically part of it, or is it general, you know, hate’s bad reported?
It is all protected classes that could be part of a bias incident.
Thank you. I’m going to turn it over–

[interposing] Chair Dinowitz– I just also want to say, you know, I’ve supervised the entire office, the dedicated Hate Crimes Office. I have an Executive Assistant District Attorney, David Kletsick [sp?], who also helps supervise these cases, and we also

learn of incidents, and sometimes during an arrest that come that we don’t think are flagged and when, you know, Chief Arias was the– in charge of hate crimes, we very clearly speak to him and say, hey, you know, we see this pattern or this case looks like it could be further investigated, and they’ve always been very willing to take a closer look. So, I think just to respond to if an officer misses it, if it’s at least– if there’s an arrest made, the District Attorney’s Early Intake Bureau will look at it, and sometimes we’ll make a referral back to the Hate Crimes Taskforce and say hey, did you guys see this case? Did you know about it? And they’ll assign a detective. And I think that also is one of the key reasons why it’s important for the District Attorney to learn about all these incidents as quickly as they take place.
Thank you for that. Thank you. I’m going to turn it over to Council Member Hanks for questions.

Thank you, Chairs. First, I want to take a moment to thank Chair Inna Vernikov and Chair Dinowitz for putting together this hearing and putting together this taskforce which I’m

a proud member to be a part of. So, my question is– so I’ve been listening, and you know, as a woman of color living in Staten Island, I mean, I know what it means to be discriminated against. I know what it means if someone is being biased towards me. But I think one of the biggest challenges that we’re seeing here is like how do I identify what a hate crime is? And then the second challenge is reporting the hate crime. Then law enforcement determining if it even rises to be a hate crime. And then we haven’t even gotten to the point of actually prosecuting them or, you know, settling when it is a hate crime, right? So, we have a lot to do, and this is probably first of many hearings. But how does NYPD tell the difference between a bias incident and a hate crime?

Sure. So, when we’re talking about a hate crime, right? Really, we’re applying New York State Penal Law, right? So, that’s a– it’s a question under state law. There’s obviously the evidentiary piece, right, the investigative work of the detectives, and then, you know, applying the law to the evidence that we have. You know, the DA was speaking in terms of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. You know, for us,

the question for an arrest is probable cause, right? And as the District Attorney said, you know, the difference for hate crimes as opposed to other crimes is it’s not just probable cause that a crime was committed and probable cause this person committed it, the probable cause that it was a hate crime, right? So, it’s a whole other layer. And in making that determination, there are a few pieces. So, one piece is that only certain crimes can qualify, can be the basis for a hate crime arrest or prosecution. There’s actually a list of offenses under New York State Law. It's a long list. Dozens and dozens of what’s called specified offenses, but it is not all crimes. So, one question is, is the criminal conduct in question a specified offense under New York State Penal Law? And if it’s not, then just as a matter of law, it can’t be a hate crime, it’s not possible. I should add, there are a few special statutes that have– in addition to the hate crime statute, there’s a few statutes that have specific references also for bias. But if none of that’s applicable, you can’t charge a hate crime. You can’t arrest for a hate crime. Then assuming that it could be a hate crime, the question is whether the person was victimized in

whole or in substantial part because of one or more protective characteristics, or the perception of that characteristic, right? So, someone attacks someone because they believe they’re Jewish– even if the person’s not Jewish, it doesn’t matter. They– that was their perception. That’s enough. I think what is important, though– I mentioned this in the testimony before, and this is a really important point, that as a matter of New York State Law– and it’s not case law, it’s actually– it’s in the statute. The identity of the perpetrator and the victim alone cannot be the basis for a hate crimes arrest. So, if someone’s attacked let’s say on the street, even if the person is visibly Jewish, that without more, with nothing more, cannot be the basis for a hate crimes arrest. And that person, of course, may perceive it that they were attacked because they’re Jewish. They may be right, but as a matter of law, there has to be some additional quantum of evidence showing that their Jewishness or perceived Jewishness was the reason why they were attacked. I mean, in terms of the investigation, again, building off what the DA said, you know, the detectives are doing really fantastic work looking,

turning over every stone, both with regard to this incident itself like talking to the complainant, talking to witnesses, pulling video, and then more broadly because of this motive pieces, learning everything they can about the suspect. Sometimes you have evidence on– you know, in the incident itself that shows you bias, right? The person used antisemitic slur. That’s incredibly powerful evidence, obviously. Sometimes, you don’t have that in the particular incident, but you have, for example, you have social media. You have statements the person made to an unrelated individual, something else, some other thing that says, oh, this is someone who is acting because of their anti-Jewish views. So, that’s a sort of overview of how they’re going about this.

Thank you so much. That was– you know, we’re still trying to get to that point where not only does law enforcement understand what a hate crime is, what a bias incident, also what is the public– what is the public’s understanding. Everybody here is on social media, so you see it. I mean, it’s palpable. It’s– again. So, that leads me to like, so how do you balance like free speech and

concerns when it comes to hate crimes. I mean, we just passed a package of bills, and there was a bit of contention there because, you know, we’re not talking about minimizing or going against free speech. However, when you’re screaming in front of a church, there’s no space for that. So, you know, how do we engage with law enforcement? It’s a multi-question. How do we engage with law enforcement, but more importantly, how are we really identifying what a hate crime is, what is a bias crime is? How are we educating the public and also educating the folks who– I may report something because I feel it was a hate crime. It’s happened. And the officer that I was reporting it to doesn’t feel it was. So, you even have that piece. So, if you can just talk a little bit about that.

Yeah, sure. Sure. There are a few different pieces to that. So, one, these are– the question whether something is– whether something is a hate crime, the question whether something is a crime at all, as opposed being protected speech, right– these are legal questions. The Legal Bureau works very, very closely with the Hate Crimes Taskforce, and actually soemthign we did

a few years ago, which I’m very proud of, is that we actually have an attorney essentially like embedded with the Hate Crimes Taskforce. So, obviously, the entire Legal Bureau is available to field questions, right, all day and night, but we actually have an attorney full-time. Her job is just this, to work directly with the detectives on their cases, to answer questions. That’s incredibly valuable, right? Just in terms of having that– knowing detectives, being much more in the weeds of the cases, that’s a very valuable thing, and again, we– obviously, the Legal Bureau, we’re happy to answer questions more generally, but having that system in place, really it points to the centrality of the legal analysis here and the sensitivity around it, and also how close the link is between Hate Crimes Taskforce and their work– and the work of the Legal Bureau.
Thank you, Council Member Hanks. Council Member Maloney?

Thank you to our Chairs. Thank you, Chair Dinowitz and Inna Vernikov. I really appreciate this taskforce. As was demonstrated in your testimony, there is clearly a rise in antisemitism and disproportionate hate crimes

affecting the Jewish population. But I was wondering if you could speak a bit to the trends in 2025 and 2026.

Sure. So, let me start with some data, then we’ll see wherever you want to go. If you look in let’s say the first quarter of 2026– right. So, you have total hate crimes in the first quarter of 2026– the total number of hate crimes, 143. The number of anti-Jewish crimes 78. So again, we’re talking– we’re talking over half. You know, we have seen that sort of north of 50 percent number for several years now. You certainly– one thing you see in the data, you know, you see a spike in 2023, and that is– I think part of that clearly is post October 7th. There’s no doubt about that. You see a spike. Bias incidents, confirmed anti-Jewish hate crimes post October 7th, and then you see that– so it goes up in 2023. Really I would say, you know, roughly constant in 2024. We’re a little bit up in 2024, and a little bit down in 2025. So, I think we had that spike. I think it has sort of leveled off in a way, but leveled off with anti-Jewish hate crimes being more than 50 percent of the hate crimes in the city. So, leveling

off is a good thing. It is, but then you have a status quo that is deeply troubling.
And we said– as you pointed out in your testimony, 10 percent of the population–
[interposing] Right, exactly.

making more than 50 percent of the hate crimes. And between January 2025 and January 2026, is it true that we’re seeing a big increase in antisemitism hate crimes, and if so, what do you attribute that to?

So, yeah, I want to speak about that. So, I’m going to use– and we’ve talked about how they’re– I want to use the confirmed hate crime numbers, because again, that’s the data of record. You do see in January of 26, relative to January 2025, a very significant spike. Here’s the thing I– here’s the thing I want to flag. In January of 2025, for whatever reason, the number of anti-Jewish crimes, confirmed anti-Jewish hate crimes, was unusually low. So, just to give you some sense of this. In 2025, looking at the confirmed hate crime data, your average number of anti-Jewish

hate crimes was 27 per month. In January of 2025, that number was 16. So, the average was 27. The number was 16 in January, 24 in February, 36 in March, 43 in April, and then it goes back down again. Now, you know, these fluctuations month-to-month, I’m not sure they– they don’t necessarily tell you very much. Obviously, you can have something happening in the world or in the city that causes a spike. Some of this is just fluctuations in crime data over time. They see this in so many crimes. Here also, because the numbers are– they’re not huge. You’re going to have huge percentage swings with small shifts. So, what you sort of see in the first quarter of 2026– the first quarter of 2026 relative to the first quarter of 2025, anti-Jewish hate crimes flat. If you look at January you see this huge spike. But again, part of that is because for whatever reason January 2025 was an unusual one.
Thank you for explaining that. I wanted to also dig into the shift in reporting.
Sure.
And curious, if this is something you’re doing for all hate crimes or just anti-Jewish hate crimes?
All hate crimes.
All hate crimes.

And it is– I think this is important, our procedures in terms of how we respond to hate crimes, how we track data, how we report data, that’s the same for all protected characteristics. We’re not distinguishing under procedures or how we report data. We’re not distinguishing between different protected classes.

And of the reported hate crimes, the percentage that are later confirmed, I’m curious for that number and if there’s a difference across different types of hate crimes? And then I’ll yield back to the Chairs.
Sure. so, I think we have that. I’ll give that to Chief Arias. I don’t know if it’s– go ahead.

So, when we look at the 2025 calendar year data, we can see that

approximately 78 percent of that reported universe resulted in confirmed hate crimes.
And that’s across all hate crimes, or just–
[interposing] Affirmative.
for anti-Jewish?
Across all hate crimes.
Thank you, Council Member Maloney. Council Member Epstein?

Thank you, Co-chairs. Thank you for holding this hearing today. It seems like the city strategy right now in preventing violence seem to not be working. We’ve seen an increase in anti-Jewish hate crimes. Really interested in figuring out what we’re all doing to reduce the amount of hate incidents. Really figuring out what evidence-based programs are in place, what’s being funded and what’s not, to make sure that we’re spending the appropriate amount of fund to do that. I’m wondering from the NYPD what prevention strategies do you have in place to education to

prevent these anti-Jewish hate crimes and the increase?

So, I guess– I mean, part of the answer to your question. It may not be the full answer, but part of the answer is I think it’s important, right, when I was saying before about how even if you have a potential bias incident, whatever happens with the Hate Crimes Taskforce–
[interposing] You know I only have a few minutes, so if you could get to– yeah.

Council Member, real quick, yes. It goes to Community Affairs, and that’s really important, right? So, Community Affairs has a role in this separate and apart from the Hate Crimes Taskforce, right, reaching out to communities to understand what’s going on, to understand the needs, to see what’s happening, to see how we can help separate and apart from the investigatory and–
So, Community Affairs you’re saying has resources to do prevention work right now?

They conduct outreach in areas where hate crimes have occurred, at the institutions in and around those locations with the victims based on policy and procedure, and it’s centralized to the Commanding Officer of the precinct of occurrence and those hate crime officers. Furthermore, we also liaison and share the incidents of hate with the Office to Prevent Hate Crimes, and you– they act as a resource, as a partner agency to the work that we do.
So, I’m going to turn to the District Attorney. Like, what resources does your office put into doing some of this prevention and community building that we’re talking about here?

Yeah, it’s a great question. Our Hate Crimes Unit in my office, again, it’s led by a woman, a senior prosecuting named Kelly Muse [sp?]. Chief Muse will attend schools or do presentaiotns. We talked a lot about such an increase of hate crimes committed among children. We see that population of young people engaging in acts of bias have been growing. There needs to be way more done in the schools. We work

with organizations like the ADL that does training, but the– one of the biggest drivers of this violence are juveniles. There’s been an increase in that, and of course, people with significant mental illness.
Okay, so more resources. You’re saying you’re not able currently to get into all the schools in the borough, but with additional resources you could expand your prevention work.
I think there’s a big key is dealing with our young offenders in this area.

I’m going to turn to the Mayor’s Office, and what resources do the Mayor’s Office put into place to kind of get in front of this? Obviously, this growth is a concern for all of us, and we want to figure out what we could be doing to do more prevention. What resources do you currently have? What resources do you need to get in front of this and prevent some of these hate crimes from happening?

Thank you, Council Member, and thank you, Chairs Vernikov and Dinowitz, for having me here Phylisa Wisdom, the

Executive Director of the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism. I’m available here for Q&A. So, the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism is just under a year old. When it was first launched it was with a staff of one. This mayor has committed to increasing the capacity of this office to be a staff of three to four, depending where we land in the Executive Budget, and our role by Executive Order is to identify and develop efforts to eliminate antisemitism and anti-Jewish hate crimes, coordinate non-law enforcement responses to antisemitic incidents, and liaise with the Jewish community and law enforcement and other agencies to improve reporting and victim services. So, our role here is really as a convener, to identify policy and programming for antisemitism prevention as well as coordinating sort of agency-wide response and liaising with the community.
And has that changed from the prior administration’s role on this?

Yes. As of now, I mean we’re talking very small numbers here, but it’s a 200 percent increase in staff capacity, and we aim to grow again by another staff member or

two, and some things are the same. So, we have an interagency taskforce that will continue to convene, but as far as policy and programming that we aim to build, that we hope will be evident to everyone here and continue to share with this taskforce what that work will look like.
What work would this taskforce do to support the work to do more prevention? Are there things you’re looking for now that we could be doing to help you prevent the rise in antisemitism?

We’re not yet ready to say specifics of what we need. We’re right now kicking off a listening tour where we’ll be talking to Jewish communities and leaders and advocates from across the five boroughs, representing the full diversity of the Jewish community and at the conclusion of that listening tour, we will have a framework in mind of how we want to use this office for the rest of the term, and as well as asking for investments in programming.
And I would encourage you to reach out to some Jewish elected officials here who would–
[interposing] Yes.
We’d love to engage with your office to hear directly from us about what we’re seeing in our communities to respond to some of the rise in antisemitism.
Absolutely, and we will be doing that very soon.
Okay, thank you.
Looking forward.
Thank you. Council Member Brewer?

Thank you to the Chairs and to everyone here. Just picking up on Council Member Epstein, I know that to the credit of the Speaker, she got funding to have eighth graders go to the Holocaust Museum which is a wonderful museum. So, I said okay, let me find out who has gone. So, I have 12 middle schools in my district and only four have attended. So, again, that’s not the only way to prevent, it’s certainly a good start. It’s more of a one-off. But I think what I’m saying is, I’ve been across the city. People are not taking

advantage of programs that could be supportive. Here’s one that’s free. I obviously will badger the other eighth graders, and they will go. But the issue is in general I want to pick up on that we’re not doing enough. So, my question is do we know– I know to the credit of the District Attorney, you said young people, people who are mentally ill, obviously anti-semites. Is that the general rule? Do we have a listing kind of who has been committing? In my district, it’s young people. That’s what I see. So, I’m just wondering, do we kind of know who the– I guess I would the knuckleheads, antisemites and mentally-ill who are doing this, and is that the kind of realm that we’re trying to educate and work with? Because prevention is what we have to focus on. Who are the knuckleheads? Who’s doing this? And the antisemites, who’s doing it?

While we don’t specifically the data of who are perpetrators are by suspect classification, we are able to see anecdotal as we review the universe of those arrested that they are precisely who you’ve described. There are youth. There are mentally-ill, and there are people who
